chapters.title_en: The Standard Measure of Knowledge — Section 1: On the Aims of the Book, the Deception of Sense and Imagination, and the Division of Knowledge
chapters.arabic_text:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
وصلى الله على سيدنا محمد وآله وسلم تسليما.
اللهم أرنا الحق حقا ووفقنا إلى اتباعه، وأرنا الباطل باطلا وأعنا على
اجتنابه.
آمين.
اعلم وتحقق أيها المقصور على درك العلوم حرصه وإرادته الممدود نحو أسرار
الحقائق العقلية همته، المصروف، عن زخارف الدنيا ونيل لذاتها الحقيرة سعيه
وكده، الموقوف على درك السعادة بالعلم والعبادة جده وجهده، بعد حمد الله
الذي يقدم على كل أمر ذي بال حمده، والصلاة على النبي محمد صلى الله عليه
وسلم رسوله وعبده.
إن الباعث على تحرير هذا الكتاب الملقب بمعيار العلم غرضان مهمان: أحدهما
تفهيم طرق الفكر والنظر، وتنوير مسالك الأقيسة والعبر؛ فإن العلوم النظرية
لما لم تكن بالفطرة والغريزة مبذولة وموهوبة كانت لا محالة مستحصلة مطلوبة،
وليس كل طالب يحسن الطلب، ويهتدي إلى طريق المطلب، ولا كل سالك يهتدي إلى
الإستكمال، ويأمن الإغترار بالوقوف دون ذروة الكمال ولا كل ظان الوصول إلى
شاكلة الصواب آمن من الإنخداع بلا مع السراب.
فلما كثر في المعقولات مزلة الأقدام، ومثارات الضلال، ولم تنفك مرآة
العقل عما يكدرها من تخليطات الأوهام وتلبيسات الخيال، رتبنا هذا الكتاب
معيارا للنظر والإعتبار، وميزانا للبحث والإفتكار، وصيقلا للذهن، ومشحذا
لقوة الفكر والعقل، فيكون بالنسبة إلى أدلة العقول كالعروض بالنسبة إلى
الشعر،
والنحو بالإضافة إلى الإعراب.
إذ كما لا يعرف منزحف الشعر عن موزونه إلا بميزان العروض ولا يميز صواب
الإعراب عن خطئه إلا بمحك النحو، كذلك لا يفرق بين فاسد الدليل وقويمه
وصحيحه وسقيمه إلا بهذا الكتاب. فكل نظر لا يتزن بهذا الميزان ولا يعيار
بهذا المعيار فاعلم أنه فاسد العيار غير مأمون الغوائل والأغوار.
والباعث الثاني الإطلاع على ما أودعناه كتاب تهافت الفلاسفة، فإنا
ناظرناهم بلغتهم وخاطبناهم على حكم اصطلاحاتهم التي تواطأوا عليها في
المنطق وفي هذا الكتاب تنكشف معاني تلك الإصطلاحات؛ فهذا اخص الباعثين
والأول أعمهما وأهمهما. أما كونه أهم فلا يخفى عليك وجهه، وأما كونه أعم
فمن حيث يشمل جدواه جميع العلوم النظرية: العقلية منها والفقهية، فإنا
سنعرفك أن النظر في الفقهيات لا يباين النظر في العقليات، في ترتيبه وشروطه
وعياره، بل في مآخذ المقدمات فقط. ولما كانت الهمم في عصرنا مائلة من
العلوم إلى الفقه بل مقصورة عليه حتى حدانا ذلك إلى أن صنفنا في طرق
المناظرة فيها مأخذ الخلاف أولا، ولباب النظر ثانيا، وتحصين المآخذ ثالثا،
وكتاب المبادي والغايات رابعا، وهو الغاية القصوى في البحث الجاري على
منهاج النظر العقلي في ترتيبه وشروطه، وأن فارقه في مقدماته
رغبنا ذلك أيضا في أن نورد في منهاج الكلام في هذا الكتاب أمثلة فقهية
فتشمل فائدته وتعم سائر الأصناف جدواء وعائدته.
ولعل الناظر بالعين العوراء نظر الطعن والإزراء، ينكر انحرافنا عن
العادات في تفهيم العقليات القطعية، بالأمثلة الفقهية الظنية فليكف عن
غلوائه في طعنه وإزرائه، وليشهد على نفسه بالجهل بصناعة التمثيل وفائدتها،
فإنها لم توضع إلا لتفهيم الأمر الخفي بما هو الأعرف عند المخاطب المسترشد،
ليقيس مجهوله إلى ما هو معلوم عنده فيستقر المجهول في نفسه.
فإن كان الخطاب مع نجار لا يحسن إلا النجر وكيفية استعمال آلاته، وجب على
مرشده ألا يضرب له المثل إلا من صناعة النجارة، ليكون ذلك أسبق إلى فهمه
وأقرب إلى مناسبة عقله وكما لا يحسن إرشاد المتعلم إلا بلغته لا يحسن إيصال
المعقول إلى فهمه إلا بأمثلة هي أثبت في معرفته؛ فقد عرفناك غاية هذا
الكتاب وغرضه تعريفا مجملا فلنزد له شرحا وإيضاحا لشدة حاجة النظار إلى هذا
الكتاب.
لعلك تقول أيها المنخدع بما عندك من العلوم الذهنية المستهتر بما يسوق
إليه البراهين العقلية، ما هذا التفخيم والتعظيم وأي حاجة بالعاقل إلى
معيار وميزان، فالعقل هو القسطاس المستقيم والمعيار القويم، فلا يحتاج
العاقل بعد كمال عقله إلى تسديد وتقويم، فلتتئد ولتتثبت فيما تستخف به من
غوائل الطرق العقلية، ولتتحقق قبل كل شيء أن فيك
حاكما حسيا وحاكما وهميا وحاكما عقليا، والمصيب من هؤلاء الحكام هو
الحاكم العقلي، والنفس في أول الفطرة أشد إذعانا وإنقيادا للقبول من الحاكم
الحسي والوهمي، لأنهما سبقا في  أول الفطرة إلى النفس وفاتحاها بالإحتكام
عليها، فألفت احتكامهما وأنست بهما قبل أن أدركها الحاكم العقلي، فاشتد
عليها الفطام عن مألوفها والإنقياد لما هو كالغريب من مناسبة جبلتها، فلا
تزال تخالف حاكم العقل وتكذبه وتوافق حاكم الحس والوهم وتصدقهما إلى أن
تضبط بالحيلة التي سنشرحها في الكتاب.
وإن أردت أن تعرف مصداق ما تقوله في تخرص هذين الحاكمين واختلالهما،
فانظر إلى حاكم الحس كيف يحكم إذا نظرت إلى الشمس عليها بأنها في عرض مجر،
وفي الكواكب بأنها كالدانير المنثورة على بساط أزرق، وفي الظل الواقع على
الأرض للأشخاص المنتصبة بأنه واقف بل على شكل الصبي في مبدأ نشئه بأنه
واقف، وكيف عرف العقل ببراهين لم يقدر الحس على المنازعة فيها، إن قرص
الشمس أكبر من كرة الأرض بأضعاف مضاعفة، وكذلك الكواكب، وكيف هدانا إلى أن
الظل الذي نراه واقفا هو متحرك على الدوام لا يفتر، وأن طول الصبي في مدة
النشء غير واقف بل هو في النمو على الدوام والإستمرار، ومترق إلى الزيادة
ترقيا خفي التدريج يكل الحس عن دركه ويشهد العقل به.
وأغاليط الحس من هذا الجنس تكثر فلا تطمع في استقصائها، واقنع بهذه
النبذة اليسيرة من أنبائه لتطلع به على أغوائه. وأما الحاكم الوهمي فلا
تغفل عن تكذيبه بموجود لا إشارة إلى جهته. وأما الحاكم الوهمي فلا تغفل عن
تكذيبه بموجود لا إشارة إلى جهته، وإنكاره شيئا لا يناسب أجسام العالم
بانفصال واتصال، ولا يوصف بأنه داخل العالم ولا خارجه. ولولا كفاية العقل
شر الوهم في تضليله هذا لرسخ في نفوس العلماء من الإعتقادات الفاسدة في
خالق الأرض والسماءن مارسخ في قلوب العوام والأغبياء.
ولا نفتقر إلى هذا الأبعاد في تمثيل تضليله وتخييله، فإنه يكذب فيما هو
أقرب إلى المحسوسات مما ذكرناه، لأنك إن عرضت عليه جسما واحدا فيه حركة
وطعم ولون ورائحة واقترحت عليه أن يصدق بوجود ذلك في محل واحد على سبيل
الإجتماع، كاع عن قبوله وتخيل أن بعض ذلك مضام للبعض ومجاور له. وقدر
التصاق  كل واحد بالآخر في مثال ستر رقيق ينطبق على ستر آخر، ولم يمكن في
جبلته أن يفهم تعدده المكان، فإن الوهم إنما يأخذ من الحس، والحس في غاية
الأمر يدرك التعدد والتباين بتباين المكان أو الزمان؛ فإذا رفعا جميعا عسر
عليه التصديق بأعداد متغايرة بالصفة والحقيقة حالة فيما هو في حيز واحد.
فهذا وأمثاله من أغاليط الوهم يخرج عن حد الإحصاء والحصر، والله تعالى
هوالمشكور على ما وهب من العقل الهادي من الضلالة، المنجي عن ظلمات
الجهالة، المخلص بضياء البرهان، عن ظلمات وساوس الشيطان.
فإن أردت مزيد إستظهار في الإحاطة بخيانة هذين الحاكمين، فدونك وإستقراء
ما ورد في الشرع من نسبة هذه التمويهات إلى الشيطان وتسميتها وسواسا
وإحالتها عليه، وتسمية ضياء العقل هداية ونورا ونسبته إلى الله تعالى
وملائكته في قوله (الله نور السموات والأرض) ولما كان مظنة الوهم والخيال
الماغ وهما منبعا الوسواس، قال أبو بكر رحمة الله عليه لمن كان يقيم الحد
على بعض الجناة: اضرب الرأس فإن الشيطان في الرأس، ولما كانت الوساوس
الخيالية والوهمية ملتصقة بالقوة المفكرة التصاقا يقل من يستقل بالخلاص
منها حتى كان ذلك كامتزاج الدم بلحومنا وأعضائنا، قال صلى الله عليه وسلم:
{إن الشيطان ليجري من ابن آدم مجرى الدم} وإذا لاحظت بعين العقل هذه
الأسرار التي نبهتك عليها استيقنت شدة حاجتك إلى تدبير حيلة في الخلاص عن
ضلال هذين الحاكمين.
فإن قلت: فما الحيلة في الإحتياط مع ما وصفتمونه من شدة الرباط بهذه
المغويات؛ فتأمل لطف حيل العقل فيه فإنه استدرج الحس والوهم إلى أمور
يساعدانه على دركها من المشاهدات الموافقة للموهوم والمعقول، وأخذ منها
مقدمات يساعده الوهم عليها ورتبها ترتيبا لا ينازع فيه، واستنتج منها
بالضرورة نتيجة لم يسع الوهم التكذيب بها، إذ كانت مأخوذة من الأمور التي
لا يتخلف الوهم والعقل عن القضاء بها، وهي العلوم التي لم يختلف فيها الناس
من الضروريات والحسيات وأستسلمها من الحس والوهم وارتهنها منهما، فصدقا بأن
النتيجة اللازمة منها صادقة حقيقة، ثم نقلها العقل  بعينها على ترتيبها إلى
ما ينازع الوهم فيه وأخرى منها نتائج.
فلما كذب الوهم بها وامتنع عن قبولها هان على العقل مؤونته، فإن المقدمات
التي وضعها كان الوهم يصدق بها على الترتيب الذي رتبه لانتاج النتيجة، فكأن
الوهم قد سلم لزوم النتيجة منها فتحقق الناظر أن آباء الوهم عن قبول
النتيجة بعد
التصديق بالمقدمات، والتصديق بصحة الترتيب المنتج لقصور في طباعه وجبلته
عن درك هذه النتيجة، لا لكون هذه النتيجة كاذبة لأن ترتيب المقدمات منقول
من موضع ساعد الوهم على التصديق بها، فإذن غرضنا في هذا الكتاب أن نأخذ من
المحسوسات والضروريات الجبلية معيارا للنظر، حتى إذا نقلناه إلى الغوامض لم
نشك في صدق ما يلزم منها. ولعلك الآن تقول: فإن تم للنظار ما ذكرتموه فلم
اختلفوا في المعقولات، وهلا اتفقوا عليها اتفاقهم على النظريات الهندسية
والحسابية التي يساعد الوهم العقل فيها؟ فجوابك من وجهين: أحدهما أن ما
ذكرناه أحد مثارات الضلال لا كلها، ووراء ذلك في النظر في العقليات عقبات
مخطرة يعز في العقلاء من يتخطاها فيسلم منها.
وإذا أحطت بمجامع شروط البرهان المنتج لليقين، لم تستبعد أن تقصر قوة
أكثر البشر عن درك حقائق المعقولات الخفية.
الثاني: ان القضايا الوهمية لما انقسمت إل ما يصدق وإلى ما يكذب وكانت
الكاذبة منها شديدة الشبه بالصادقة، اعترض فيها قضايا إعتاض على النفس
تمييزها عن الكاذبة، ولم يقو عليها إلا من أيده الله بتوفيقه وأكرمه بسلوك
منهاج الحق بطريقه، فانقسمت العقليات إلى ما هان دركها على الأكثر، وإلى ما
استعصى على عقول الجماهير إلا على الشذاذ من أولياء الله تعالى المؤيدين
بنور الحق الذين لا تسمح الإعصار الطويلة بوجود الآحاد منهم، فضلا عن العدد
الكثير الجم.
ولعلك الآن تحسب نفسك واحدا من غمار الناس فتتلو على نفسك سورة اليأس،
وتزعم أني متى أكون واحد الدهر، فريد العصر، مؤيدا بنور الحق متخلصا عن
نزغات الشيطان مستوليا على وصفته من شروط البرهان؛ فالركون إلى الدعة أولى
بي والقناعة بالإعتقاد الموروث من الآباء أسلم  لي من أن أركب متن الخطر
ولست أثق بنيل قاصية الوطر، فيقال في مثالك، إن خطر هذا ببالك: ما أنت إلا
كإنسان لاحظ رتبة سلطان الزمان وما ساعده من الشوكة والعدة والنجدة والثروة
والأشياع والأتباع، والأمر المتبع المطاع، واستبعد أن ينال رتبته أو يقارب
درجته، والأمر المتبع المطاع، واستبعد أن ينال رتبته أو يقارب درجته، ولكن
اقتدر أن ينال رتبة الوزارة أو رتبة الرئاسة أو منزلة أخرى دونها فقال:
الصواب لي بعد العجز عن الغاية القصوى، والذروة العليا التي هي درجة سلطان
الدنيا أن أقنع بصناعة الكنس التي هي صناعة آبائي، فالكناس ليس يعجز عن خبز
يتناوله وثوب يستره إقتداء بقول الشاعر:
دع المكارم لا ترحل لبغيتها ... واقعد فإنك أنت الطاعم الكاسي
وهذا الخسيس القاصر النظر، لو أنعم الفكر وتأمل واعتبر علم أن بين درجة
الكناس والسلطان منازل فلا كل من يعجز عن الدرجات العلي ينبغي أن يقنع
بالدركات السفلى، بل إذا انتهض مترقيا عن رتبة الخساسة، فما يترقى إليه
بالإضافة إلى ما يترقى عنه رياسة - فهكذا ينبغي أن تعتقد درجات السعادة بين
العلماء، فما منا إلا له مقام معلوم لا يتعداه، وطور محدود لا يتخطاه، ولكن
ينبغي أن يشوف إلى أقصى
مرقاه، وأن يخرج من القوة إلى الفعل كل ما تحتمله قواه. فإن قلت: إني
فهمت الآن شدة الحاجة إلى هذا الكتاب بما أوضحته من التحقيق، ثم اشتدت
رغبتي بما أوردته من التشويق، واتضح لي غايته وثمرته فأوضح لي مضمونه.
فاعلم أن مضمونه تعليم كيفية الإنتقال من الصور الحاصلة في ذهنك إلى
الأمور الغائبة عنك. فإن هذا الإنتقال له هيئة وترتيب إذا روعيت أفضت إلى
المطلوب، وإن أهملت قصرت عن المطلوب، والصواب من هيئته وترتيبه شديد الشبه
بما ليس بصواب. فمضمون هذا العلم على سبيل الإجمال هذا، وأما على سبيل
التفصيل فهو أن المطلوب هو العلم، والعلم ينقسم إلى العلم بذوات الأشياء،
كعلمك بالإنسان والشجر والسماء وغير ذلك. ويسمى هذا العلم تصورا، وغلى
العلم بنسبة هذه الذوات المتصورة بعضها  إلى بعض إما بالسلب أو بالإيجاب،
كقولك الإنسان حيوان والإنسان ليس بحجر، فإنك تفهم الإنسان والحجر فهما
تصوريا لذاتهما، ثم تحكم بأن أحدهما مسلوب عن الآخر أو ثابت له، ويسمى هذا
تصديقا لأنه يتطرق إليه التصديق والتكذيب.
فالبحث النظري بالطالب إما أن يتجه إلى تصو أو إلى تصديق، والموصل إلى
التصور يسمى قولا شارحا فمنه حد ومنه رسم، والموصل إلى التصديق يسمى حجة
فمنه قياس ومنه استقراء وغيره. ومضمون هذا الكتاب تعريف مبادىء القول
الشارح لما أريد تصوره حدا كان أو رسما، وتعريف مبادىء الحجة الموصلة إلى
التصديق قياسا كانت أوغيره مع لا تنبيه على شروط صحتها ومثار الغلط فيهما.
فإن قلت: كيف يجهل الإنسان العلم التصوري حتى يفتقر إلى الحد؟ قلنا بأن
يسمع الإنسان إسما لا يفهم معناه كمن قال: ما الخلاء وما الملاء وما الملك
وما الشيطان وما العقار؟ فتقول: العقار هو الخمر، فإن لم يفهمه باسمه
المعروف أفهمه بحده. وقيل: إن الخمر شراب معتصر من العنب مسكر، فيحصل له

- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "knowledge, perception, cognition" — the impression of a thing's form upon the mind; also "a sign/mark by which something is known."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ʿilm is the apprehension of a thing as it truly is (idrāk al-shayʾ ʿalā mā huwa bihi), contrasted with jahl (ignorance); it is the highest human perfection and the means to saʿādah (felicity).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — the mind's grasp of a form; metaphorical (majāz) — ʿilm as "light" (nūr) guiding to truth, as in the Quranic verse cited herein.
- Root: ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To look, consider, reflect"; naẓar is the act of intellectual scrutiny and deliberation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for rational inference — the orderly movement of thought from premises to conclusion; the foundation of theoretical science (al-ʿulūm al-naẓariyyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical sight; metaphorical — intellectual insight and reasoning (taʾammul), as in "the eye of reason" (ʿayn al-ʿaql).
- Root: و-ه-م (w-h-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To imagine, conjecture"; wahm is the estimative faculty that judges particulars without rational proof.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, wahm is the faculty that often errs, judging by sensory semblance rather than intellectual necessity; it must be subordinated to ʿaql.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — mental supposition; metaphorical — the "whispering" (waswās) of Satan, as it leads the soul astray from rational truth.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-Ḥāl wa al-Tamyīz (The Circumstantial Accusative and Specification) — The opening invocation uses vocative and optative constructions (Allāhumma arinā...), followed by complex conditional and causal clauses (idh, lammā, fa-inna) that require careful parsing of the apodosis and protasis to preserve the logical flow of the author's argument.
chapters.translation:
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. And may God bless our master Muhammad, his family, and grant them abundant peace.

O God, show us truth as truth and grant us success in following it, and show us falsehood as falsehood and aid us in avoiding it. Amen.

Know and ascertain — O you whose striving and will are confined to the attainment of sciences, whose aspiration is stretched toward the secrets of rational verities, whose effort and toil are turned away from the embellishments of this world and the attainment of its base pleasures, whose earnestness and exertion are devoted to the attainment of felicity through knowledge and worship — after praising God, whose praise precedes every matter of consequence, and blessing the Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, His messenger and servant:

Indeed, the motives for composing this book, entitled *The Standard Measure of Knowledge*, are two important aims: The first is to make understood the ways of thought and reflection, and to illuminate the paths of syllogisms and proofs. For since the theoretical sciences are not bestowed and granted by nature and instinct, they are necessarily acquired and sought after. But not every seeker excels at seeking, nor is every seeker guided to the path of the sought object; nor is every traveler guided to completion, nor safe from being deceived by stopping short of the summit of perfection; nor is everyone who thinks he has reached the likeness of correctness safe from being deluded by the mirage's false glitter.

Since, in the realm of intelligibles, the slippage of feet has multiplied, and the sources of error have proliferated, and the mirror of reason has never been free of what clouds it — namely, the confusions of fancies and the obscurations of imagination — we have arranged this book as a standard measure for reflection and consideration, a scale for investigation and meditation, a polisher for the mind, and a whetstone for the power of thought and reason. It stands in relation to the proofs of intellects as prosody stands in relation to poetry, and as grammar stands in relation to inflection.

For just as the defective meter of poetry is not known from its sound one except by the measure of prosody, and the correctness of inflection is not distinguished from its error except by the touchstone of grammar, so too the corrupt from the sound, and the valid from the invalid, among arguments is not distinguished except by this book. So every reflection that is not weighed by this scale, nor measured by this standard — know that it is of corrupt measure, not safe from perils and depths.

The second motive is to provide access to what we have deposited in the book *The Incoherence of the Philosophers*. For we have debated them in their own language and addressed them according to the dictates of their technical conventions upon which they have agreed in logic. And in this book, the meanings of those conventions are disclosed. So this is the more specific of the two motives, while the first is the more general and the more important of them. As for its being more important, its aspect is not hidden from you. As for its being more general, it is so in that its benefit encompasses all theoretical sciences — both the rational and the jurisprudential. For we shall make known to you that reflection in jurisprudential matters does not differ from reflection in rational matters in its arrangement, conditions, and standard measure, but only in the sources of its premises.

And since the aspirations of our age have inclined from the sciences toward jurisprudence — nay, have become confined to it — this has driven us to compose, on the methods of disputation therein: first, *The Source of Disagreement*; second, *The Core of Reflection*; third, *The Fortification of Premises*; and fourth, *The Book of Principles and Ends*, which is the ultimate goal in inquiry conducted according to the method of rational reflection in its arrangement and conditions, even if it differs from it in its premises. This also moved us to include, in the method of discourse in this book, jurisprudential examples, so that its benefit might be comprehensive and its utility encompass all classes of disciplines.

Perhaps the viewer with the squinting eye — the eye of criticism and disparagement — will deny our deviation from custom in teaching certain rational truths through probable jurisprudential examples. Let him desist from his excess in criticism and disparagement, and let him testify against himself of ignorance of the art of analogy and its benefit. For analogy was not established except to make understood a hidden matter through what is more familiar to the guided interlocutor, so that he may compare his unknown to what is known to him, and thus the unknown becomes settled in his mind.

For if the discourse is with a carpenter who excels only in carpentry and the use of its tools, it is incumbent upon his guide not to strike an example for him except from the craft of carpentry, so that it may be more readily grasped by his understanding and closer to the suitability of his mind. And just as it is not proper to guide a learner except in his own language, so too it is not proper to convey the intelligible to his understanding except through examples that are most firmly established in his knowledge. We have thus made known to you, in a summary fashion, the ultimate aim of this book and its purpose. Let us now add to this an explanation and clarification, given the intense need of the reflective thinkers for this book.

Perhaps you will say — O you who are deluded by what you possess of mental sciences, and who are reckless with what rational proofs drive you toward — "What is this magnification and glorification? And what need does a rational person have for a standard measure and a scale? For reason is the straight balance and the upright standard. The rational person, after the perfection of his reason, has no need for correction and straightening." Then be deliberate and be steadfast regarding what you take lightly of the perils of rational paths, and ascertain before everything that within you there is a sensory judge, an estimative judge, and a rational judge. The one who is correct among these judges is the rational judge.

The soul, at the beginning of its natural constitution, is most yielding and submissive to acceptance from the sensory and estimative judges, because they precede the rational judge in the soul's early constitution and begin their jurisdiction over it. So the soul becomes accustomed to their jurisdiction and familiar with them before the rational judge reaches it. Thus, weaning it from what it is accustomed to, and submitting to what is, as it were, a stranger to the suitability of its innate constitution, becomes difficult for it. It does not cease to contradict the rational judge and deny him, while agreeing with the sensory and estimative judges and affirming them — until it is restrained by the stratagem that we shall explain in this book.

If you wish to know the confirmation of what we say regarding the delusion of these two judges and their corruption, then look at the sensory judge: how it judges, when you look at the sun, that it is the breadth of a handspan or so; and at the stars, that they are like scattered dinars upon a blue carpet; and at the shadow falling upon the ground from upright figures, that it is stationary; and at the form of a child at the beginning of its growth, that it is stationary. And how reason has known, through proofs that sense is unable to contest, that the disk of the sun is many times larger than the sphere of the earth — and likewise the stars. And how it has guided us to the fact that the shadow we see as stationary is in perpetual motion, never resting, and that the height of the child during the period of growth is not stationary but is continuously and persistently increasing, rising toward increase with a rise so subtly gradual that sense is wearied by perceiving it, while reason testifies to it.

The errors of sense of this kind are numerous — do not aspire to exhaust them. Be content with this small sample of its reports, to become aware through it of its misleading. As for the estimative judge, do not neglect to deny it regarding an existent to which no direction can be pointed, and its denial of something that does not suit the bodies of the world by separation and connection, and that cannot be described as inside the world nor outside it. Were it not for reason's sufficiency against the evil of imagination in this misleading of it, there would have become entrenched in the minds of scholars corrupt beliefs concerning the Creator of the heavens and the earth, just as they are entrenched in the hearts of the common folk and the dull-witted.

Nor do we need this remoteness in exemplifying its misleading and its illusion-making. For it denies what is closer to the sensibles than what we have mentioned. For if you present to it a single body in which there is motion, taste, color, and odor, and you propose to it that it affirm the existence of all that in a single locus by way of conjunction, it recoils from accepting it and imagines that some of that is adjacent to and contiguous with the rest. It supposes each one to be attached to the other, like a thin veil covering another veil. And it is not possible in its innate constitution to understand their multiplicity in a single place. For imagination only takes from sense, and sense, at the utmost, perceives multiplicity and distinction by the distinction of place or time. So when both are removed, it becomes difficult for it to affirm numbers that are distinct in attribute and essence, subsisting in what occupies a single spatial extent.

This and its like, of the errors of imagination, exceed the bounds of enumeration and limitation. And God, exalted be He, is the One thanked for what He has bestowed of reason — the guide from error, the deliverer from the darknesses of ignorance, the rescuer, by the light of proof, from the darknesses of Satan's whisperings.

If you desire further reinforcement in encompassing the treachery of these two judges, then take up and survey what has come in the Sacred Law of attributing these deceptions to Satan and naming them "whisperings" (waswās), and referring them to him; and naming the light of reason "guidance" and "illumination," and attributing it to God and His angels, in His saying: {«Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth»} (Quran 24:35). And since the locus of imagination and fancy is the brain — the two being the source of whisperings — Abu Bakr, may God have mercy on him, said to one who was carrying out the prescribed punishment on some offender: "Strike the head, for Satan is in the head." And since the imaginative and estimative whisperings cling to the thinking faculty with a clinging from which few are able to free themselves — so much so that it is like the mingling of blood with our flesh and limbs — he, peace be upon him, said: {«Indeed, Satan flows through the son of Adam like the flow of blood»} (Bukhari, Muslim). And when you observe with the eye of reason these secrets to which we have alerted you, you will be certain of your intense need to devise a stratagem for deliverance from the error of these two judges.

If you say: "Then what is the stratagem for caution, given what you have described of the intensity of the bond with these misleading things?" — then contemplate the subtlety of reason's stratagem therein. For it has lured sense and imagination to matters in which they assist it in apprehending — namely, observed things that accord with the imagined and the rational. From these it took premises that imagination assists it in affirming, arranged them in an order that is not contested, and deduced from them, by necessity, a conclusion that imagination was unable to deny — since it was taken from matters concerning which imagination and reason do not differ in judgment. These are the sciences about which people have not differed: the necessary and the sensory. Reason received them from sense and imagination and held them as pledges from them. So they affirmed that the conclusion entailed by them is true in reality. Then reason transferred that very same arrangement to what imagination contests, and deduced from it other conclusions.

When imagination denied these and refused to accept them, its burden became light for reason. For the premises that reason had laid down, imagination affirmed them in the order in which they were arranged for producing the conclusion. So it was as if imagination had conceded the entailment of the conclusion from them. Thus the reflective thinker ascertained that imagination's refusal to accept the conclusion — after affirming the premises and affirming the correctness of the productive arrangement — was due to a deficiency in its nature and constitution for grasping this conclusion, not because the conclusion is false. For the arrangement of the premises is transferred from a place where imagination assisted in affirming them. So, then, our purpose in this book is to take from the sensibles and the innate necessities a standard measure for reflection, so that when we transfer it to the obscure matters, we do not doubt the truth of what follows from them.

Perhaps you will now say: "If what you have mentioned is accomplished for the reflective thinkers, then why have they differed regarding the intelligibles? And why have they not agreed upon them as they have agreed upon the geometrical and arithmetical theoretical matters, in which imagination assists reason?" Your answer is from two aspects: The first is that what we have mentioned is one of the sources of error, not all of them. Beyond that, in reflection upon the intelligibles, there are perilous obstacles that it is rare among the rational to cross and thus be saved from. And when you encompass the totality of the conditions of the demonstrative proof that produces certainty, you will not deem it unlikely that the power of most human beings falls short of grasping the hidden verities of the intelligibles.

The second: Since the estimative propositions are divided into what is true and what is false, and the false ones among them are intensely similar to the true ones, propositions arose therein that were difficult for the soul to distinguish from the false. None prevailed over them except one whom God aided with His grace and honored with the pursuit of the path of truth by its way. Thus the intelligibles were divided into what was easy for the majority to grasp, and what was intractable to the minds of the masses — except for the rare few among the friends of God, aided by the light of truth, whom long epochs do not permit the existence of even single individuals among them, let alone a great and numerous multitude.

Perhaps you now count yourself as one of the common crowd, and recite to yourself the chapter of despair, claiming: "When shall I be the unique one of the age, the peerless of the era, aided by the light of truth, delivered from the incitements of Satan, mastering the full description of the conditions of demonstration? So leaning toward ease is better for me, and contentment with the inherited belief of the fathers is safer for me than riding upon the back of danger, while I do not trust in attaining the far-reaching goal." So it is said regarding your example — if this crosses your mind: You are nothing but like a man who observed the rank of the sultan of the age, and what he was granted of might, equipment, valor, wealth, partisans, and followers, and the obeyed and followed command — and deemed it unlikely to attain his rank or approach his station. But he was able to attain the rank of vizier, or the rank of leadership, or another station below it. Then he said: "The correct course for me, given my incapacity for the ultimate goal and the highest summit, which is the rank of the sovereign of the world, is to be content with the craft of sweeping — which is the craft of my fathers. For the sweeper is not incapable of bread to eat and a garment to cover himself," following the poet's saying:

*Leave noble deeds, do not journey in pursuit of them, and sit — for you are the eater and the clothed.*

This base and short-sighted man — if he reflected deeply, contemplated, and took heed, he would know that between the rank of the sweeper and the sultan there are stations. Not everyone who is incapable of the highest ranks should be content with the lowest depths. Rather, if he rises, ascending from the rank of baseness, what he ascends to — in relation to what he ascends from — is a leadership. Thus should you believe regarding the degrees of felicity among the scholars. For there is none among us but has a known station that he does not exceed, and a determined limit that he does not cross. But one should aspire to the utmost of his ascent, and bring from potentiality to actuality all that his powers can bear.

If you say: "I have now understood the intense need for this book, by what you have clarified of the verification; then my desire has intensified by what you have presented of the encouragement; and its ultimate aim and fruit have become clear to me. So clarify for me its content." — Then know that its content is the teaching of the manner of transition from the forms present in your mind to the matters absent from you. For this transition has a form and an arrangement: if they are observed, they lead to the sought object; if neglected, they fall short of it. And the correct of its form and arrangement is intensely similar to what is not correct. So the content of this science, in summary, is this. As for in detail, it is that the sought object is knowledge, and knowledge is divided into knowledge of the essences of things — like your knowledge of man, tree, sky, and other than that. This knowledge is called "conception" (taṣawwur). And into knowledge of the relation of these conceived essences to one another, either by negation or affirmation — like your saying "Man is an animal" and "Man is not a stone." For you understand "man" and "stone" — these are two conceptions of their essences — then you judge that one is negated of the other or affirmed of it. This is called "assent" (taṣdīq), because affirmation and denial pertain to it.

So the theoretical inquiry of the seeker is directed either toward conception or toward assent. That which leads to conception is called an "explanatory statement" (qawl shāriḥ): of it there is the definition (ḥadd) and the description (rasm). That which leads to assent is called an "argument" (ḥujjah): of it there is the syllogism (qiyās), induction (istiqrāʾ), and other than that. The content of this book is the definition of the principles of the explanatory statement for what is intended to be conceived — whether definition or description — and the definition of the principles of the argument leading to assent — whether syllogism or other — along with the alerting to the conditions of their validity and the sources of error in both.

If you say: "How does a person become ignorant of conceptual knowledge such that he needs the definition?" — We say: It is when a person hears a name and does not understand its meaning, like one who asks: "What is khalāʾ? What is mulāʾ? What is malak? What is shayṭān? What is ʿuqār?" So you say: "ʿUqār is wine." If he does not understand it by its known name, you make him understand it by its definition. For it is said: "Wine is an intoxicating beverage pressed from grapes," and thus he obtains a conceptual knowledge of the essence of wine. As for assentive knowledge, it is when a person is ignorant, for example, that the world has a Maker. He says: "Does the world have a Maker?" You say: "Yes, the world has a Maker," and you make known to him the truth of that by the argument and the proof, as we shall clarify. This, then, is the content of the book.

And if you wish to know the index of the chapters: Know that we have divided the discourse on the means of knowledge into four books: The Book of the Premises of the Syllogism, the Book of the Syllogism, the Book of the Definition, and the Book of the Divisions of Existence and Its Judgments.

The first book concerns the premises of the syllogism. Let us mention an introduction by which the aspect of the division of inquiry in the syllogism — from the least to the greatest — is known. We say: The farthest aim in this section is the demonstration (burhān) that yields certain knowledge. And demonstration is a type of syllogism, for "syllogism" is a general name, while "demonstration" is a specific name for a type of it. The syllogism is not composed except of two premises, and each premise is not composed except of a subject (mawḍūʿ) and a predicate (maḥmūl). And every subject or predicate mentioned in a proposition is a word that necessarily indicates a meaning. So the syllogism is composite. And every inquirer into a composite thing — his way is to analyze the composite into its simples and begin inquiry into the units, then into the composite. Thus, from inquiry into the syllogism follows inquiry into what the syllogism resolves into — namely, the premises; and from inquiry into the premises follows inquiry into the predicate and subject from which the premises are composed; and from inquiry into the predicate and subject follows inquiry into the individual words and meanings by which the predicate and subject are completed. And from inquiry into the premises follows inquiry into their conditions. For every composite of matter and form, one must inquire into its matter and its form. This is nothing but like one who wishes to build a house: his due is to attend to the separation of the materials from which it is composed — like bricks, clay, and wood — then to occupy himself with the shaping and the manner of arrangement and composition. Likewise is inquiry into the syllogism. This, then, is the explanation of the need for these divisions. Let us now proceed to the intended subject.

The first art of the Book of Premises: On the indication of words and the exposition of the aspects of their indication and their relation to meanings. Its exposition is through seven divisions:

The first division: We say that words indicate meanings in three distinct aspects. The first aspect is indication by way of correspondence (muṭābaqah) — like a name posited for a thing, such as the word "wall" indicating the wall. The second is by way of inclusion (taḍammun) — like the word "house" indicating the wall, and the word "man" indicating the animal; likewise the indication of every more specific attribute upon the more general essential attribute. The third is indication by way of implication and entailment (iltizām) — like the word "ceiling" indicating the wall, for it entails it as a necessary concomitant external to its essence; and the word "man" indicating the capacity for the craft of tailoring and learning it. What is considered valid in definitions is the indication of correspondence and inclusion. As for the indication of entailment, it is not — because it is not what the language-positor posited, unlike the other two. For the indicated meaning therein is neither delimited nor circumscribed, since the concomitants of things and the concomitants of their concomitants cannot be restricted nor enumerated. This would lead to the word being an indicator of an infinite number of meanings, which is impossible.

The second division: On the word with respect to the generality and specificity of its meaning. The word is divided into the particular (juzʾī) and the universal (kullī). The particular is that whose very conception of its meaning prevents the occurrence of sharing in its concept — like your saying "Zayd," "this tree," and "this horse." For what is conceived from the word "Zayd" is a specific person whom no other shares in being the meaning of the word "Zayd." The universal is that whose very conception of its meaning does not prevent the occurrence of sharing in it. If sharing is prevented, it is prevented by something external to its very concept and the requirement of its word — like your saying "man," "horse," and "tree." These are names of genera, species, and universal general meanings. This usage runs in the Arabic language in every noun upon which the definite article "al-" enters, not in the context of reference to a previously known specific referent — like "the man" (al-rajul). For it is a generic name: you may utter it intending a specific man whom the addressee knew before, saying "The man came," where the "al-" is for definition — i.e., the man who came to me before. But when there is no such contextual indicator, the name "man" is a universal name in which every individual of men shares in being subsumed under it.

If you say: "When we say 'the spherical form encompassing twelve constellations' — and there exists in actuality no form with this attribute except one — how is the name universal while the named is one, given that the 'al-' has entered, which necessitates the inclusion of all individuals under it?" — It is said to you: This is universal, for we do not stipulate that what is subsumed under it exists in actuality. Rather, it is permissible that it exists in potentiality and possibility. And were its existence supposed, it would necessarily be subsumed under it. And before existence, it is subsumed — unlike the name "Zayd," for sharing in it is impossible both in actuality and in potentiality.

If you say: "When we say 'the True God' — how is this universal, while sharing in it is prevented both in actuality and potentiality? Likewise our saying 'the sun,' according to one who does not permit the existence of another sun — for what is subsumed under it is determined as the determination of the person of Zayd in conception from the word 'Zayd'?" — It is said to you: The word is universal, and the prevention of sharing in it is not due to the very concept of the word and its subject matter, but due to a meaning external to it — namely, the impossibility of the existence of two gods for the world. And we have not stipulated in the word's being universal except that the very concept of the word and its subject matter not prevent the occurrence of sharing in it. So there has been obtained for you, from the two questions and their answers, that the universal is of three divisions: A division in which sharing exists in actuality — like our saying "man" when its individuals exist; a division in which sharing exists in potentiality — like our saying "man" if it happened that no individual remained in existence except one, and the sphere encompassing twelve constellations, since there exists only one; and a division in which there is no sharing, neither in actuality nor in potentiality — like "God," and it is nonetheless universal, because the prevention is not from the subject matter of the word and its predicate, unlike the word "Zayd."

chapters.arabic_text:
### | فائدة فقهية

قد اختلف الأصوليون في أن الإسم المفرد إذا اتصل به الألف واللام هل
يقتضي الإستغراق، وهل ينزل منزلة العموم كقول القائل الدينار أفضل من
الدرهم والرجل خير من المرأة، فظن الظانون أنه من حيث كونه اسما فردا لا
يقتضي الإستغراق لمجرده، ولكن فهم العموم بقرينة التسعير وقرينة التفضيل
للذكر على الأنثى، إنما هو لعلمنا بنقصان الدرهمية عن الدينارية ونقصان
الأنوثة عن الذكورة. وأنت إذا تأملت ما ذكرناه في تحقيق معنى الكلي، فهمت
زلل هؤلاء بجهلهم أن اللفظ الكي يقتضي الإستغراق بمجرده ولا يحتاج إلى
قرينة زائدة فيه. فإن قلت: ومن أين وقع لهم هذا الغلط؟ فستفهم ذلك من
القسمة الثالثة.

### | القسمة الثالثة في بيان رتبة

### | الألفاظ من مراتب الوجود

إعلم أن المراتب فيما نقصده أربعة واللفظ في الرتبة الثالثة، فإن للشيء
وجودا في الأعيان ثم في الأذهان، ثم في الألفاظ ثم في الكتابة.
فالكتابة دالة على اللفظ واللفظ دال على المعنى الذي في النفس، والذي في
النفس هو مثال الموجود في الأعيان،
فما لم يكن للشيء ثبوت في نفسه لم يرتسم في النفس مثاله. ومهما ارتسم في
النفس مثاله فهو العلم به، إذ لا معنى للعلم إلا مثال يحصل في النفس مطابق
لما هو مثال له في الحس وهو المعلوم، وما لم يظهر هذا الأثر في النفس لا
ينتظم لفظ يدل به على ذلك الأثر، وما لم ينتظم اللفظ الذي ترتب فيه الأصوات
والحروف لا ترتسم كتابة للدلالة عليه. والوجود في الأعيان دالتان بالوضع
والإصطلاح.
وعند هذا نقول: من زعم أن الإسم المفرد لا يقتضي الإستغراق ظن انه موضوع
بإزاء الموجود في الأعيان فإنها أشخاص معينة إذ الدينار الموجود شخص معين،
فإن جمعت أشخاص سميت دنانير، ولم يعرف أن الدينار الشخصي المعين يرتسم
منهفي النفس أثر هو مثاله وعلم به وتصور له، وذلك المثال يطابق ذلك الشخص
وسائر اشخاص الدنانير الموجودة والممكن وجوها، فتكون الصورة الثابتة في
النفس من حيث مطابقتها لكل دينار يفرض صورة كلية لا شخصية؛
فإن اعتقدت أن إسم الدينار دليل على الأثر في النفس لا على المؤثر وذلك
الأثر كلي، كان الإسم كليا لا محالة، وما قدمناه من الترتيب يعرفك أن
الألفاظ لها دلالات على في النفوس، وما في النفوس مثال لما في الأعيان
وسيأتي مزيد للعاني الكلية المرتسمة في النفوس بسبب مشاهدة الأشخاص الجزئية
في كتاب أحكام الوجود ولواحقه.

### | القسمة الرابعة للفظ

### | قسمته من حيث إفراده وتركيبه

اعلم أن اللفظ ينقسم إلى مفرد ومركب، والمركب ينقسم إلى مركب ناقص وغلى
مركب تام، فهي ثلاثة أقسام:

### | الأول

هو المفرد وهو الذي لا يراد بالجزء منه دلالة على شيء أصلا حين هو جزؤه
كقولك عيسى وإنسان، فإن جزئي عيسى وهما " عي وسا " وجزئي إنسان وهما " إن
وسان " مايراد بشيء منهما الدلالة على شيء أصلا. فإن قلت: فما قولك في عبد
الملك؟ فاعلم أنه أيضا مفرد إذا جعلته إسما علما كقولك زيد، وعند ذلك لا
تريد بعبد دلالة على معنى ولا بالملك دلالة على معنى. فكل منهما من حيث هو
جزؤه لا يدل على شيء فيكونان كأجزاء
إسم زيد وهما إسمان في الصورة جعلا إسما واحدا كبعلبك ومعد يكرب، فإن
اتفق أن يكون المسمة به عبدا للملك تحقيقا فيكون هذا الإسم مطلقا عليه من
وجهين: احدهما في تعريف ذاته فيكون الإسم مطلقا عليه من وجهين: أحدهما في
تعريف ذاته فيكون الإسم مفرادا، والآخر في تعيف صفته في عبودية الملك فيكون
قولك عبد الملك وصفا له فيكون مركبا لا مفردا، فافهم هذه الدقائق فإن مثار
الأغاليط في النظريات تنشأ من إهمالها.
والمركب التام هو الذي كل لفظ منه يدل على معنى والمجموع بدل دلالة تامة
بحيث يصح السكوت عليه، فيكون من إسمين ويكون من إسم وفعل. والمنطقي يسمى
الفعل كلمة والمركب الناقص بخلافه.
فقولك: زيد يمشي والناطق حيوان؛ مركب تام، وقولك: في الدار أو انسان؛
مركب  ناقص لأنه مركب من إسم وأداة لا من إسمين ولامن إسم وفعل، فإن مجرد
قولك " زيد في " أو " زيد لا " لا يدل على المعنى الذي يراد الدلالة عليه
في المحاورة ما لم يقل زيد في الدار أو زيد لا يظلم، فإنه بذلك الإقتران
والتتميم يدل دلالة تامة بحيث يصح السكوت عليه.

### | القسمة الخامسة للفظ المفرد في نفسه

اللفظ إما إسم أو فعل أو حرف. ولنذكر حد كل واحد على شرط المنطقيين
لتنكشف أقسامه، فنقول: الإسم صوت دال بتواطؤ مجرد عن الزمان والجزء من
أجزائه لا يدل على إنفراده ويدل على معنى محصل، ولما كان الحد، مكربا من
الجنس والفصول وتذكر الفصول للاحترازات، كان قولنا صوت جنسا، وقولنا دال
فصلا يفصله عن العطاس والنحنحنة والسعال وأمثالها، وقولنا بتواطؤ يفصله عن
نباح الكلبح فإنه صوت دال على ورود وارد لكن لا بتواطؤ، وقولنا مجرد عن
الزمان نحو قولنا يقوم وقام وسيقوم، فإن كل واحد صوت دال بتواطؤ، وقولنا
الجزء من أجزائه لا يدل على إنفراده احترازا عن المركب التام كقولنا زيد
حيوان، فإن هذا يسمى خبرا وقولا لا إسما، وقولنا يدل على معنى محصل احترازا
عن الأسماء التي ليست محصلة كقولنا لا إنسان، فإنه محصل احترازا عن الأسماء
التي ليست محصلة كقولنا لا إنسان، فإنه لا يسمى إسما مع وجود جميع أجزاء
الحد فيه سوى هذا الإحتراز.
فإن قولنا لا إنسان قد يدل على الحجر والسماء والبقر، وبالجملة على كل
شيء ليس بإنسان
فليس له معنى محصل، إنما هو دليل على نفي الإنسان لا على إثبات شيء.
وأما الفعل وهو الكلمة فإنه صوت دال بتواطؤ على الوجه الذي ذكرناه في
الإسم، إنما يباينه في أنه يدل على معنى وقوعه في زمان كقولنا قام ويقوم،
وليس يكفي في كونه فعلا أن يدل على الزمان فحسب؛ فإن قولنا أمس واليوم وغدا
وعام أول ومضرب الناقة ومقدم الحاج يدل على الزمان، وليس بفعل، حيث أن
الفعل يدل على معنى وزمان يقع فيه المعنى فيكون الفعل  أبدا دليلا على معنى
محمول على غيره، فإذن الفرق بين الإسم والفعل تضمن معنى الزمان فقط.
وأما الحرف وهو الأداة فهو كل ما يدل على معنى لا يمكن أن يفهم بنفسه ما
لم يقدر اقتران غيره به، مثل من وعلى وما أشبه ذلك.
وقد أوجز هذه الحدود فقيل في الإسم: إنه لفظ مفرد يدل على معنى من غير أن
يدل على زمان وجود ذلك المعنى من الأزمنة الثلاثة، ثم منه ما هو محصل كزيد
ومنه ما هو غير محصل، كما إذا اقترن به حرف سلب فقيل لا إنسان.
والكلمة هي لفظة مفردة تدل على معنى وعلى الزمان الذي ذلك المعنى موجود
فيه لموضوع ما غير معين، والحرف أو الأداة ما لا يدل على معنى باقترانه
بغيره.

### | القسم السادسة في نسبة الألفاظ إلى المعاني

إعلم أن الألفاظ من المعاني على أربعة منازل: المشتركة والمتواطئة
والمترادفة والمتزايلة.
أما المشتركة فهي اللفظ الواحد الذي يطلق على موجودات مختلفة بالحد
والحقيقة إطلاقا متساويا كالعين تطلق على العين الباصرة، وينبوع الماء وقرص
الشمس وهذه مختلفة الحدود والحقائق.

- Root: ك-ل-ل (k-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes totality, encompassment, and that which gathers all parts without exception.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, al-kullī (the universal) is the intellectual form that applies to all individuals of a kind, as opposed to the partial (juzʾī); istighrāq (exhaustive inclusion) is its linguistic correlate in the context of generality (ʿumūm).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage of al-istighrāq is the exhaustive coverage of all members; metaphorical (majāz) usage would be its application to a restricted set without a qualifying indicator (qarīnah).
- Root: ر-س-م (r-s-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To trace, sketch, or imprint a form; the act of leaving a mark or impression.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In epistemology, irtisām is the imprinting of the form of the known object in the soul, which constitutes knowledge (ʿilm) itself—the correspondence (muṭābaqah) between the mental image and the external existent.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage refers to physical tracing; metaphorical usage is the intellectual impression of a quiddity in the mind, as employed here by the author.
- Root: و-ض-ع (w-ḍ-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To place, set down, or establish; the act of positing a thing in a specific position.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the science of language, al-waḍʿ is the conventional positing of a linguistic form (lafẓ) to signify a meaning (maʿnā), whether by mutual agreement (iṣṭilāḥ) or divine convention (tawqīf).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is physical placement; metaphorical usage is the conventional assignment of a word to its signification, as in the author's phrase "dāllatān bi-al-waḍʿ wa-al-iṣṭilāḥ."
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Composition (Qāʿidat al-Tarkīb) — A complete sentence (kalām tāmm) is that which yields a complete benefit (faʾidah) and upon which silence is permissible (yaṣiḥḥu al-sukūt ʿalayhi), whereas an incomplete composition (murakkab nāqiṣ) fails to convey full signification without supplementation.
chapters.translation:
### | A Juridical Benefit

The scholars of uṣūl (legal methodology) have differed as to whether the single noun (al-ism al-mufrad), when the definite article alif-lām is attached to it, necessitates exhaustive inclusion (al-istighrāq), and whether it is placed in the rank of generality (al-ʿumūm)—as when one says, "The dinar is better than the dirham," and "The man is superior to the woman." Those who held this mistaken view supposed that, insofar as it is a single noun, it does not necessitate exhaustive inclusion by its mere self, but rather that the understanding of generality arises from the indicator of valuation (qarīnat al-tasʿīr) and the indicator of preference (qarīnat al-tafḍīl) of the male over the female—this being only due to our knowledge of the deficiency of dirham-ness relative to dinar-ness, and the deficiency of femininity relative to masculinity. But if you contemplate what we have set forth concerning the verification of the meaning of the universal (al-kullī), you will understand the slip of these persons, owing to their ignorance that the universal word necessitates exhaustive inclusion by its mere self, without needing any additional indicator. If you say: "Whence did this error occur to them?"—you will understand that from the third division.

### | The Third Division: Elucidating the Rank of Words Among the Ranks of Existence

Know that the ranks with respect to what we intend are four, and the word (al-lafẓ) occupies the third rank. For a thing has an existence in external entities (al-aʿyān), then in minds (al-adhhān), then in words (al-alfāẓ), then in writing (al-kitābah). Thus writing is indicative of the word, and the word is indicative of the meaning that is in the soul (al-nafs), and that which is in the soul is the likeness (mithāl) of the existent in external entities. So unless a thing has stability (thubūt) in itself, its likeness is not imprinted in the soul. And whenever its likeness is imprinted in the soul, that is knowledge of it (al-ʿilm bihi), for there is no meaning of knowledge except a likeness that obtains in the soul corresponding to that of which it is a likeness in sensation (al-ḥiss)—and that is the known object (al-maʿlūm). And unless this impression (al-athar) appears in the soul, no word is composed to indicate that impression; and unless the word is composed, in which sounds and letters are ordered, no writing is imprinted for indicating it. Thus existence in external entities has two indicators: by convention (al-waḍʿ) and by agreement (al-iṣṭilāḥ).

At this point we say: Whoever claims that the single noun does not necessitate exhaustive inclusion supposes that it is posited in correspondence to the existent in external entities, for these are particular individuals (ashkhāṣ muʿayyanah)—since the existing dinar is a particular individual. If you gather individuals, they are called dinars. But he does not know that from the particular dinar, a specific individual, there is imprinted in the soul an impression that is its likeness, and knowledge of it, and conceptualization (taṣawwur) of it. And that likeness corresponds to that individual and to all other individuals of dinars, both existent and possible in their modes (wujūh). Thus the form established in the soul, by virtue of its correspondence to every dinar that may be supposed, is a universal form (ṣūrah kulliyyah), not a particular one (shakhṣiyyah). So if you hold that the name "dinar" is indicative of the impression in the soul, not of the impressor (al-muʾaththir), and that impression is universal, then the name is necessarily universal. And what we have presented of the ordering will make known to you that words have indications of what is in the souls, and what is in the souls is a likeness of what is in external entities. Further elaboration of the universal meanings imprinted in the souls by reason of observing particular individuals will come in the book "The Judgments of Existence and Its Corollaries" (Aḥkām al-Wujūd wa-Lawāḥiqihi).

### | The Fourth Division of the Word: Its Division in Terms of Its Singleness and Composition

Know that the word is divided into the single (mufrad) and the composite (murakkab). The composite is divided into the incomplete composite (murakkab nāqiṣ) and the complete composite (murakkab tāmm). Thus they are three divisions:

### | The First

It is the single (al-mufrad), which is that of which no part is intended to indicate anything at all insofar as it is a part of it—as when you say "ʿĪsā" and "insān" (man). For the two parts of ʿĪsā, namely "ʿī" and "sā," and the two parts of insān, namely "in" and "sān," nothing of them is intended to indicate anything at all. If you say: "What do you say concerning ʿAbd al-Malik?" Know that it too is single if you make it a proper name (ism ʿalam), like your saying "Zayd." In that case, you do not intend by "ʿabd" an indication of a meaning, nor by "al-malik" an indication of a meaning. Thus each of them, insofar as it is a part of it, does not indicate anything, so they are like the parts of the name "Zayd"—two names in form, made into one name, like "Baʿlabakk" and "Maʿdīkarib." But if it happens that the one named is truly a slave of the king (ʿabd li-al-malik), then this name is applied to him from two aspects: one is in defining his essence (taʿrīf dhātihi), in which case the name is single; the other is in defining his attribute of servitude to the king, in which case your saying "ʿAbd al-Malik" is a description of him, and thus it is composite, not single. So grasp these subtleties, for the source of fallacies in theoretical matters arises from neglecting them.

The complete composite is that of which every word indicates a meaning, and the totality indicates a complete signification such that silence upon it is permissible (yaṣiḥḥu al-sukūt ʿalayhi). It may be composed of two nouns, or of a noun and a verb. The logician calls the verb "kalimah" (word), and the incomplete composite is contrary to that. Thus your saying "Zayd walks" and "The rational is an animal" is a complete composite. Your saying "In the house" or "a man" is an incomplete composite, because it is composed of a noun and a particle (adāh), not of two nouns, nor of a noun and a verb. For merely your saying "Zayd in" or "Zayd not" does not indicate the meaning intended in discourse (al-muḥāwarah) unless you say "Zayd is in the house" or "Zayd does not wrong," for by that conjunction and completion it indicates a complete signification such that silence upon it is permissible.

### | The Fifth Division of the Single Word in Itself

The word is either a noun (ism), a verb (fiʿl), or a particle (ḥarf). Let us mention the definition (ḥadd) of each, on the condition of the logicians, so that its divisions may be disclosed. We say: The noun is a sound (ṣawt) indicating by mutual convention (bi-tawāṭuʾ), devoid of time (mujarrad ʿan al-zamān), of which no part indicates anything by its isolation, and which indicates a determinate meaning (maʿnā muḥaṣṣal). Since the definition is composed of genus (jins) and differentiae (fuṣūl), and the differentiae are mentioned for exclusions (iḥtirāzāt), our saying "sound" is a genus; our saying "indicating" is a differentia separating it from sneezing, throat-clearing, coughing, and the like; our saying "by mutual convention" separates it from the barking of a dog, for it is a sound indicating the arrival of an arriver, but not by mutual convention; our saying "devoid of time" is like our saying "he stands" (yaqūm), "he stood" (qāma), and "he will stand" (sayaqūm), for each of these is a sound indicating by mutual convention; our saying "of which no part indicates anything by its isolation" is an exclusion of the complete composite, like our saying "Zayd is an animal," for this is called a report (khabar) and a statement (qawl), not a noun; our saying "which indicates a determinate meaning" is an exclusion of nouns that are not determinate, like our saying "no man" (lā insān), for it is not called a noun despite the presence of all parts of the definition in it, save this exclusion. For our saying "no man" may indicate stone, sky, and cow—in sum, everything that is not a man. Thus it has no determinate meaning; it is only an indicator of the negation of man, not of the affirmation of anything.

As for the verb (al-fiʿl), which is the kalimah, it is a sound indicating by mutual convention in the manner we mentioned for the noun, but it differs from it in that it indicates a meaning whose occurrence (wuqūʿ) is in a time—like our saying "he stood" (qāma) and "he stands" (yaqūm). It is not sufficient for its being a verb that it merely indicate time; for our saying "yesterday" (ams), "today" (al-yawm), "tomorrow" (ghadan), "last year" (ʿām awwal), "the she-camel's milking place" (maḍrib al-nāqah), and "the pilgrim's arrival" (muqaddam al-ḥājj) indicate time, yet are not verbs. For the verb indicates a meaning and a time in which that meaning occurs, so the verb is always an indicator of a meaning predicated (maḥmūl) upon something else. Thus the difference between the noun and the verb is the inclusion of the meaning of time alone.

As for the particle (al-ḥarf), which is the tool (al-adāh), it is everything that indicates a meaning that cannot be understood by itself unless the conjunction of something else with it is supposed—like "min" (from), "ʿalā" (upon), and the like. These definitions have been summarized, and it was said concerning the noun: It is a single word indicating a meaning without indicating the time of the existence of that meaning among the three times. Then of it there is the determinate, like "Zayd," and the non-determinate, as when a particle of negation is conjoined to it, and it is said "no man." The kalimah is a single word indicating a meaning and the time in which that meaning exists for some unspecified subject (mawḍūʿ ghayr muʿayyan). The particle, or tool, is that which does not indicate a meaning except by its conjunction with something else.

### | The Sixth Division: The Relation of Words to Meanings

Know that words, in relation to meanings, are in four stations: the equivocal (al-mushtarakah), the univocal (al-mutawāṭiʾah), the synonymous (al-mutarādifah), and the divergent (al-mutazāyilah). As for the equivocal, it is the single word applied to existents differing in definition (ḥadd) and reality (ḥaqīqah) with an equal application—like "ʿayn" (eye), applied to the seeing eye, the spring of water, and the disk of the sun, these being different in definitions and realities.
